newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA CURRENT ACCOUNT - Review of forecasts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA CURRENT ACCOUNT - Review of forecasts.

text.p: Australia's current account deficit for November will be released at 11.30 a.m. (0030 GMT).
It is the first major piece of data of the year, and should help shake off some of the Christmas and New Year cobwebs.
The median forecast of the 24 economists Reuters surveyed was for a current account deficit of A$1.75 billion. Forecasts ranged from A$1.5 billion to A$1.9 billion.
The median expectation is under the October deficit of A$1.788 billion, despite the already published 1.2 percent rise in merchandise imports in the past month.

Economists said exports would most likely post a stronger rise than imports in the month, after only partially retracing September's 2.9 percent fall in October.

That September fall ended a three-month run of trade surpluses, and if the trade balance is to return to surplus in November, imports will need to rise by at least 1.6 percent. Such a rise, however, would only take exports back to where the were in August.
Not all agreed that exports would rise however, and those tipping a fall in exports saw a widening current account that could place the Australian dollar under some pressure.

Economists also said that while the current account had improved in 1996, and receded as a market concern, it was mainly because of the cyclical nature of the trade baalnce and the underlying nature of the current account deficit remained unchanged.

ANZ economists said that the A$1 billion imporvement in the monthly current account deficit since the 1995 peak had shifted the deficit out of the limelight, but question the prudence of this waning interest.
The monthly deficit remains propped up by the net income deficit -- in seven of the first 10 months of 1996, the net income deficit was actually larger than overall current account deficit.
"If the current account deficit concerned you in early 1995, it probably should now too," the ANZ economists said in a commentary.
